  advisory in this release and become validation warnings in the next, so a
  manifest that loaded before this change still loads.

Make the three settings in the block do what the schema says:

- `unmanifested_nodes` now reaches the merge pipeline. `error` keeps the
  gateway serving and reports the undeclared nodes on `GET /health`; it
  never claimed a startup abort in code, only in prose.
- `inherit_runtime_resources: false` keeps a linked app to the resources it
  declares, including when its id matches the bound node's name
- `allow_manifest_override: false` demotes the manifest layer's field
  groups, and an explicitly configured per-group merge policy still wins

All three survive a manifest reload instead of freezing at startup, and
reading the effective policy no longer takes the manifest-load lock, so a
reload cannot stall the liveness path.

Stop the merge from rewriting an entity's `source`. Provenance decides
whether the orphan filter may delete an entity, so a field-group policy
must not be able to reassign it: with the manifest layer demoted for
metadata, a declared entity was retagged and then deleted, and the same
configuration is reachable through the gateway parameters alone.

Decide deletion by the layer that owns an entity rather than by the string
in `source`. A discovery plugin may set its own tag - two shipped plugins
use "beacon" and "opcua" - and those were not covered by the "plugin"
prefix, so `ignore` erased them. Layer ownership is already tracked during
the merge; the filters now consult it. No `source` value changes, which
matters because one capability is gated on the literal "node" and the
opcua tag carries a trust distinction.

On `GET /health`, `warnings` and `warning_schema_version` are now emitted
whenever the gateway can produce a warning, not only under aggregation, and
both are required in the schema. Warning objects keep identifier domains
apart: `entity_ids` carries addressable SOVD entity ids for every code, and
ROS node names live in `ros_node_fqns`. A Component id announced by a peer
is validated before it is published there. `discovery.linking` reports the
configured policy so a monitor can act on it without parsing prose.

Register integration feature tests with CONFIGURE_DEPENDS. Without it a
test file added to an existing build tree is never registered, and the
suite reports success without running it. For the same reason, the
incremental clang-tidy filter now considers staged and working-tree changes
as well as committed ones.

The new integration tests use the shared scaled time budgets, so their
deadlines widen under a sanitizer the same way the rest of the suite's do.
Poll intervals and soak durations stay unscaled: an interval is not a budget,
and stretching a soak would hold the gateways longer under exactly the
instrumentation that makes them expensive.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
docs: describe first_occurred as the start of the current occurrence

first_occurred is reset when a FAILED event reactivates a CLEARED fault, so it
marks the start of the latest occurrence rather than the fault's first report
ever. Both backends do this deliberately (fault_storage.cpp:155-158,
sqlite_fault_storage.cpp:437-441, written back in the UPDATE at :485-492), and
both pin it in tests: test_fault_manager.cpp:402/423 and
test_sqlite_storage.cpp:480/501 assert the timestamp moves to the reactivating
report.

Fault.msg, the msgs README and the API reference all said "when the fault was
first reported". That is wrong the same way the occurrence_count wording was,
and the two fields are read together: with occurrence_count now trustworthy as
an edge counter, pairing it with first_occurred to get a rate gives an answer
that is wrong precisely because the timestamp moved with the last edge.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
docs: describe occurrence_count as the edge counter it is

occurrence_count counts occurrence edges: the first FAILED event, and each
FAILED that arrives while the fault is CLEARED. Repeated FAILED events inside
one occurrence leave it alone and advance last_occurred instead.

Fault.msg, the msgs README and the API reference all described it as the total
number of FAILED events across all sources. The fault_manager README and design
doc said it keeps updating during the latch window, which contradicted the
storage header that states the opposite.

FaultEvent.msg, the gateway README and the report handler also gave
occurrence_count as an example of what fault_updated carries. It is not among
those fields, since a re-report inside one occurrence does not change it.

The wording for the latch window is taken from FaultStorage's own header so the
three places that describe it now read the same.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
test(cmake): assert the guard suppresses exactly the launch tests, not just something

cmake_guard.py's assert_guard_suppressed_launch_tests only required that
some baseline test disappeared and some guarded test survived - a guard
that also swallowed a package's gtests would still pass, as long as its
pytest coverage alone kept the surviving set non-empty. Identify the
baseline's actual launch tests by the `python3 -m launch_testing.launch_test`
marker every add_launch_test()-generated command carries (LABELS cannot be
used for this: real launch tests override the "launch_test" default to
whatever the caller passed), and assert the guarded set is exactly the
baseline minus those - proven against the coordinator's own mutation
(medkit_add_gtest silently skipping test_rosbag_capture under system-package
conditions): the old assertions pass it, the new one fails it with the exact
missing test named. One legitimate exception exists and is now explicit:
ros2_medkit_integration_tests' own test_launch_test_guard_system_build gates
its own registration on the same guard signal, for reasons unrelated to
being a launch test, and the new assertion takes an also_suppressed
parameter to say so instead of silently mismatching.

Also: declared ament_cmake_gtest as a test_depend of ros2_medkit_cmake -
GTEST_PROBE calls find_package(ament_cmake_gtest REQUIRED) and this suite
runs in the Humble binarydeb chroot (it is a pytest test, which the guard
does not suppress), so an undeclared dependency there would have added a
new failure to the log this branch exists to clean. Checked every other
find_package a probe issues against package.xml; the rest were already
declared. Added the probe this would have needed: two boundary cases the
guard's prefix and localstatedir comparisons let slip through today
(/usr/ros/humble, and /var/lib plus /variable) now expect registration and
would fail against a broadened regex. Added a check for
cmake_parse_arguments' KEYWORDS_MISSING_VALUES in medkit_add_launch_test,
so a value that happens to spell another keyword's name (e.g. LABELS "ENV")
fails the configure instead of silently vanishing. Narrowed three comments
that promised ENV can never overwrite MEDKIT_TEST_DOMAINS without
qualifying that the check is a literal-string match, not a
generator-expression evaluation. Documented that the probes rely on
AMENT_PREFIX_PATH/CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH being inherited from the farm's own
`. setup.sh` before dh_auto_test runs. Updated design/index.rst: the
ROS2MedkitTestDomain.cmake module inventory now documents the guard instead
of describing medkit_add_launch_test as unconditional, and the "keep
test-only find_package calls out of this package" decision now reconciles
with the probes this branch adds, which comply with the reason behind that
rule (each declares its own C/CXX project) while looking like they violate
its literal wording.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(cmake): declare ament_cmake_gtest for the new gtest probe

GTEST_PROBE in test_launch_test_guard.py calls
find_package(ament_cmake_gtest REQUIRED), but package.xml never
declared it as a test_depend. test_launch_test_guard is registered
with ament_add_pytest_test, which the guard deliberately does not
suppress, so this suite runs in the Humble binarydeb chroot - where
the probe's own configure would fail on the undeclared dependency and
add a new failure to the exact log this branch exists to clean. Every
CI image already carries ament_cmake_gtest, which is why CI stayed
green.

Checked every other find_package a probe issues (ament_cmake,
launch_testing_ament_cmake, ament_cmake_pytest) against package.xml;
all three were already declared.

Also: documented that the probes rely on AMENT_PREFIX_PATH and
CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH being inherited from the farm's own `. setup.sh`
before dh_auto_test runs, and why ROS_DISTRO is the one export missing
from that same environment. Corrected cmake_guard.py's docstring,
which claimed its assertions prove a system-package configure
suppressed "exactly the launch tests and nothing else" - they don't;
that narrower claim is what the gtest and pytest probes prove in
isolation. Updated design/index.rst: the ROS2MedkitTestDomain.cmake
module inventory now documents the system-package guard instead of
describing medkit_add_launch_test as registering unconditionally, and
the "keep test-only find_package calls out of this package" decision
now reconciles with the probes this branch adds, which comply with the
reason behind that rule (each declares its own C/CXX project, so the
NONE-language hazard the rule exists for does not apply to them) while
looking like they violate its literal wording.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(cmake): stop the launch-test guard from reading ROS_DISTRO

The guard returned early (registering launch tests) whenever ROS_DISTRO
was unset in the environment, which is exactly the state of the ROS
build farm's binarydeb chroot - no in-tree package.xml depends on
ros_environment, the only source of that export outside a Docker
image's own ENV, and the farm's chroot install log carries neither.
The guard never fired in the job it exists for.

Drop the environment dependency entirely: the install-prefix check is
now a wildcard match against /opt/ros/<anything>, decided purely from
CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX and CMAKE_INSTALL_LOCALSTATEDIR, both of which
colcon never sets. Added a probe that deletes ROS_DISTRO from the
child environment and still expects suppression - it fails against the
prior guard and passes against this one. The two real-configure tests
that built their system-package prefix from ROS_DISTRO now use a
literal instead, since any distro name proves the same thing against
the new wildcard match.

Also: dropped the CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX trailing-slash normalisation,
which CMake performs itself before project code ever runs (confirmed
on 3.22, 3.28, 4.4) and which left that probe unable to fail either
way; repointed the probe at CMAKE_INSTALL_LOCALSTATEDIR's trailing
slash instead, which is the comparison that actually needed one. Added
a gtest probe alongside the existing pytest one, since the shared
suppressed-launch-tests assertion only proves something non-empty
survived, not specifically a gtest. Added a configure-time check that
every entry in the per-test timeout override list actually matched a
discovered test, so a renamed or deleted test file fails the configure
instead of silently losing its timeout budget. Corrected two doc
passages left stale by the same reasoning (README ownership claims for
launch-test properties the macro never set, and a package.xml comment
naming a package count and behavior that changed in an earlier round).

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
build(cmake): own launch-test properties in the macro and skip them in a system package build

A launch test resolves its own package through the ament index, which only an
installed prefix carries, while a system package build runs the test step before
the install step. Every launch test in the tree therefore failed in the Humble
binarydeb job, and because bloom runs that step as `dh_auto_test || true` the
failures could not stop the build, so what shipped was a published log full of
errors that said nothing about the package.

Skipping registration alone was not enough. Callers named the test afterwards to
set labels and environment, and properties on a test that does not exist fail the
configure outright. `medkit_add_launch_test` now takes `LABELS`, `ENV` and `ARGS`
and applies them itself, after the domain and by appending, which also removes the
trap where a plain `set_tests_properties(... ENVIRONMENT ...)` dropped the domain
and left the test on domain 0. Every call site across seven packages moved onto it.

Registration is then skipped when the install prefix is the ROS distribution root
and debhelper's `CMAKE_INSTALL_LOCALSTATEDIR` is `/var`. Either signal alone has a
false positive: the prefix also matches `colcon build --install-base`, and
`include(GNUInstallDirs)` defines the variable as a relative `var`. gtests and
pytest tests are deliberately untouched, because that chroot is the only place our
packages are exercised against a minimal dependency closure.

The guard is proven by running a real cmake configure of every package that
registers launch tests and requiring it to succeed, rather than by matching text.
`ros2_medkit_graph_watchdog` cannot be a dependency of the integration test package
without a cycle, so it runs the same check in its own suite instead of being
covered by accident. Neither test can skip: where it is registered, it asserts.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
test: scale the shared wall-clock budgets with the sanitizer time factor

get_time_scale() exists for budgets asserted inside a test: the sanitizer jobs
rewrite every ctest TIMEOUT by the same factor, but a "must answer within N
seconds" assertion in the test body never saw it, so sanitizer overhead reads as
a regression in the code. None of the seven shared budgets used it.

PARAM_SERVICE_TIMEOUT carries the evidence that this already bit someone: its
comment says a parameter service was still answering 503 more than 15 s into a
TSan run, and it was raised to 90 by hand instead.

The polling intervals are deliberately left alone. They are not budgets, and a
slower poll under a sanitizer would only notice later that the thing it waits
for is ready.

Nothing changes without MEDKIT_TEST_TIME_SCALE, which only the sanitizer jobs
set: the factor is 1.0 everywhere else, so the normal jobs keep the tight
budgets that give the assertions their falsifying power.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix: the log bridge swallowed two parameters, one of them a NaN

max_tracked_nodes was clamped to [1, INT_MAX] with nothing in the log, so a
config asking for 0 ran at 1 and the file and the process disagreed in silence.

report_cooldown_sec was worse than silent. The check read "negative -> 0.0", and
every comparison against NaN is false, so NaN passed it, then passed the
"<= 0 disables the cooldown" test in cooldown_allows, and reached
Duration::from_seconds - where converting NaN to nanoseconds is undefined. The
window built from it then suppresses either every ERROR report or none, with no
way to tell which from outside. It is now isfinite plus a positive range test,
in the same shape as the sibling float checks.

Both are pinned by a second bridge in the integration test carrying 0 and NaN.
Reverting either fix fails it.

The two rows in the config page said "clamped to at least 1" and "a negative
value disables it"; both now describe what the code does.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix: isolate the four gateways, and close the mutation gaps the tests left open

The clamp test launches four gateways and was registered for one DDS domain, so
each of them ran discovery over the other three's nodes and four sets of
participants expired on that domain at teardown. Nothing here is a peer of
anything else. It joins the multi-gateway list and each gateway gets its own
domain, which is what that list exists for.

The polling helper added for the orphan e2e race dropped its sleep on the wrong
branch. poll_faults returns the moment it matches the code, BEFORE its own
sleep, so the present-but-incomplete path - the one the helper exists for -
became a bare retry loop against the gateway whose detector it is waiting on.
The sleep is now on that branch, where it belongs.

Mutation gaps closed, each of them a fix this branch makes that no test pinned:

- triggers.max_triggers was only tested with -1, which narrows to -1 and trips
  the same branch, so reverting the read-before-narrow order stayed green. It
  now carries a value above INT_MAX like its six siblings.
- fault_manager.service_timeout_sec was tested with NaN, but NaN already fails
  "> 0" on its own. +inf is the value that passes the comparison and is caught
  only by isfinite - and the one that would reach wait_for_service.
- topic_sample_timeout_sec had no value below 0.1, so deleting that term was a
  green mutation. The two ends now sit on different gateways.
- PARAMS_FLOOR_ONLY was computed and never used, so setting one more row's
  ceiling to None silently dropped its coverage. It is asserted now.
- Every assertion read a warning and none read the result. Three sites log the
  value they installed, so the refusal defaults are checked rather than believed.

The orphan assertions pinned two topic names independently, which a regression
pairing either with something else would satisfy. They pin the pair phrase now.

Docs: the fault-trigger subsection had been spliced between the Triggers table
and its example; the note claiming the table matches gateway_params.yaml
contradicted the row this branch corrected; troubleshooting carried a third
value for the sample timeout; four parameters enumerated under "Out-of-range
values" documented no range, which is that section's own precondition; and the
YAML header duplicated a parameter list that had already drifted - it now points
at the one place that carries it.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
test: wait for the pair by name instead of for the fault code

test_orphan_e2e asserted that one aggregated GRAPH_ORPHAN description names two
different pub/sub pairs, but it only waited for the fault code to appear.

The detector raises as soon as its FIRST pair crosses the persistence gate and
rewrites the description on later ticks as more pairs cross it. The two pairs in
this fixture are discovered independently over DDS and cross the gate on
different ticks, so the code exists well before both are named. poll_faults
returns the moment the code is there, which is why a slower runner read a
description carrying only the LaserScan pair and failed on the namespace one.

Both assertions had the mirrored version of the same race: whichever pair
crossed first decided which test failed.

poll_fault_describing waits until the description names the pairs the test is
about. Reproduced on demand by delaying the second publisher by 8 s: the old
form fails with the same message CI produced, the new one waits and passes.

The description cap gets a note with the measured numbers - 449 characters of
480 with these topic names - because a rename that pushes it over truncates a
pair and looks exactly like the race that is now gone.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix: stop pinning rclcpp's NaN handling for a range-descriptor parameter

parameter_service_timeout_sec carries a FloatingPointRange descriptor, and what
rclcpp does with NaN against it differs by distribution. Jazzy accepts NaN as
in-range, verified on a running gateway that logged "timeout=nans". Lyrical
refuses it, and the process exits 1 before reaching our own check - which is
what the new test row asserted against, so CI went red there.

The row is gone. Asserting either outcome pins rclcpp's behaviour rather than
ours. The gateway's isfinite check stays: on the distributions that accept NaN
it is the only thing between NaN and a duration cast.

The docs and the code comment now state the split instead of describing Jazzy's
behaviour as universal.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix: close the remaining silent-coercion holes, including NaN past a range descriptor

triggers.max_triggers had the same shape as the size_t holes already fixed here,
one subsystem over: read site narrows to int, TriggerManager compares against a
size_t. triggers.max_triggers:=-1 gave a bound of 18446744073709551615, so the
documented "HTTP 503 when this limit is reached" never fired and triggers could
be added over the REST API without end. Checked as int64 before narrowing.

fault_manager.service_timeout_sec was never validated. std::max(x, 0.0) does not
filter NaN - the comparison is false, so NaN comes back out - and NaN then
reaches wait_for_service, where the duration cast is undefined and the result is
treated as wait-forever: one fault RPC pins an HTTP worker for the life of the
process. A non-positive value is the quiet version: every fault call answers
"service not available" with nothing logged.

parameter_service_timeout_sec and parameter_service_negative_cache_sec are
declared with a FloatingPointRange descriptor, and the config docs said rclcpp
therefore rejects a bad value outright. True except for NaN: that check compares
with < and >, both false for NaN, so the gateway started with "timeout=nans" and
carried it into a duration cast and a try_lock_for. Verified on a running
gateway. They are now checked for finiteness at the read.

sse.max_duration_sec reported "must be > 0" for a value that plainly is greater
than zero; the branch is [1, INT_MAX] and the message now says so. It also
logged under the node logger while the two clamps beside it use the rest_server
logger, which is the one the config docs show operators.

keep_alive_timeout_sec was logged with %ld and a cast to long; std::time_t is
not guaranteed to fit, so both the warning and the info line now use int64_t.

Tests. aborted_severity and dedup_capacity had no test at all: the action status
bridge integration test now launches a second bridge carrying both values above
INT_MAX and asserts each warning names the supplied value. Reverting either fix
fails it, with the log showing the wrapped aborted_severity=2.

The NaN fix for topic_sample_timeout_sec was equally unpinned - 60.0 was the
only value fed, and the old comparison rejects it identically. NaN does survive
the launch path, checked against a running gateway, so it is now a row of its
own, with the plain out-of-range value kept separately: one pins the finiteness
guard, the other pins the range.

Docs. The Fault-trigger rules section had been spliced into the middle of the
Triggers table, leaving triggers.on_restart_behavior and triggers.storage.path
as rows of the fault_triggers table. discovery.manifest_strict_validation was
described as rejecting a manifest that fails validation; validation errors abort
the load whatever it is set to, and the flag only decides whether warnings are
fatal.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix: close a NaN hole, two narrowing holes, and a race in the new test

topic_sample_timeout_sec let NaN through. The check read "below 0.1 or above
30.0", and every comparison against NaN is false, so NaN reached both consumers
as a sampling timeout. It is now an isfinite check plus the range as a positive
test. Do not let a linter rewrite that back: the two forms are not equivalent
for NaN, and clang-tidy suggests exactly that rewrite.

aborted_severity and dedup_capacity in the action status bridge were declared as
int, so a ROS int64 parameter was narrowed before its range check and wrapped
back into the accepted band: 4294967298 became 2 and passed as ERROR in silence.
Both are read as int64 and checked before narrowing, and the warning now names
the value that was actually supplied.

The new integration test anchored its output scan on "TopicDataProvider
attached", emitted by main.cpp before it starts the fault-trigger engine. The
fault_triggers.poll_interval_ms warning is emitted after that, so the scan could
read a buffer that did not have it yet. Measured in a real run: old anchor at
line 164, the warning at 169, four milliseconds apart. The anchor is now the
engine's own startup line, which comes after every assertion target.

Config docs corrected where they described something the code does not do:

- severity_floor: DEBUG and INFO never become faults whatever it is set to, so
  0, 10 and 20 all behave like 30
- report_cooldown_sec: keyed by fault code and severity, not by node, and
  applied to ERROR and FATAL only
- rosbag.storage_path: an empty value falls back to the system temp directory,
  not to the snapshot storage
- fault_triggers.poll_interval_ms: read only when the engine actually starts, so
  with no plugin a mis-set value is neither applied nor reported

The test docstring claimed the skipped above-ceiling case buys only a log line.
It also buys the only check on three ceiling constants: widening
http_thread_pool_size from 1024 to 8 leaves every test here green while the docs
still advertise 1024. Said plainly now.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
docs: document the parameters the config reference never mentioned

An audit of every declare_parameter call against docs/config found four groups
with no documentation at all.

The fault manager's audit_log group (enabled, transitions, retention_max_records,
fail_closed, database_path) gets a section. fail_closed needed the caveat
spelled out: it does not roll back the fault-state change that triggered the
transition, because that change has already committed to a separate database and
the two cannot be made atomic. It signals a broken audit chain, nothing more.

Four rosbag parameters appeared only inside an example block, never in the
parameter table: include_topics, exclude_topics, format and storage_path.

The log bridge and the action status bridge had no config page at all, 18
parameters between them. Both now have one, including what each does when the
value is refused.

keyvalue_codes is added to the diagnostic bridge page.

critical_immediate_confirm was described as global-only and not overridable
per-entity, which reads as a parameter. It is not one: critical faults skipping
debounce is built in and cannot be configured at all.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix: report the fault-trigger poll interval, and correct the config docs

fault_triggers.poll_interval_ms was floored to 50 ms with nothing in the log,
which is the same silent coercion the rest of this branch removes. It is now
clamped with a warning, and validated as int64 before it is narrowed to int for
the timer.

The test helper joined process output chunks with a newline. Those chunks are
raw stream slices, not lines, so a boundary landing inside a log line spliced a
newline into the message and a substring match on it failed while the line was
plainly there. It surfaced under a sanitizer, where the timing moved the
boundary. Concatenation reconstructs the stream.

Config docs corrected against the code:
- cors.allowed_origins default is an empty list, not [""]
- cors.allowed_methods default includes POST and DELETE
- topic_sample_timeout_sec declares 1.0; gateway_params.yaml sets 2.0, so a
  bare run and a launch that loads it differ. Both are now stated.
- max_parallel_topic_samples does not exist. The table row was already replaced
  by data_provider.max_parallel_samples; the example block and the
  troubleshooting page still carried it.
- aggregation.max_discovered_peers documents its 1-1000 range.

Parameters that had no documentation at all: discovery.manifest_strict_validation
and discovery.manifest.fragments_dir get rows in the discovery page, and the
fault_triggers.* group gets a section in the server page.

The test covers fault_triggers.poll_interval_ms in all three directions. Reaching
it needs a loaded plugin, so the gateways now load the test plugin.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix: catch the startup parameters that were still absorbed silently

The first commit covered the parameters that are clamped. Several others are
validated in a different way and were still silent, or were checked in an order
that let the value through.

Read before narrowing. server.port, refresh_interval_ms and sse.max_duration_sec
were narrowed from int64 to int and only then range-checked, so a value above
INT_MAX wrapped back into the legal band and was accepted without a word:

  server.port:=4294976296  ->  listens on 9000, nothing logged

Each is now validated as int64 first, and the warning names the value that was
refused instead of the wrapped one.

No more wrapping to SIZE_MAX. sse.max_subscriptions, bulk_data.max_upload_size
and aggregation.max_discovered_peers were cast straight to size_t. A negative
value became a huge one, so the documented limit stopped existing: no HTTP 503
at the subscription cap, no bound on uploads, no cap on discovered peers. They
are now checked and reported.

topic_sample_timeout_sec is validated at the read. Both consumers fell back to
1.0 on their own, but DataAccessManager lives in the ROS-neutral core and cannot
log, so a value rejected there vanished. Their fallbacks stay as contract
guards; the read site is the one that reports.

Docs said one thing and the code does three. The note claiming every documented
range is clamped to the nearest endpoint was wrong for a third of the ranges in
the same file, and server.rst contradicted itself 320 lines apart. It now
describes the three real behaviours: clamped, refused in favour of the
documented default, or rejected by rclcpp so the gateway does not start.
max_parallel_topic_samples is documented but does not exist in the code; it is
replaced by the real data_provider.max_parallel_samples. The nine
subscription_executor.* and data_provider.* knobs get config rows, so the note's
premise ("a parameter that documents a valid range") holds for them too.

The test gains two gateways. One sets every clamped parameter to a legal value
and must report nothing: without it, a site that lost its "did the clamp fire"
guard would warn at every boot of a correctly configured gateway and no
assertion would notice. The other carries the refused values.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix: report every clamped startup parameter

A startup parameter set outside its documented range was coerced to the
nearest endpoint without a word in the log. The config file and the running
process then disagreed with nothing to show it, and the symptom of a wrong
value (a slow or jittery gateway) shows up far from the cause.

Every clamped parameter now logs the requested and the effective value, in
the shape three of them already used:

  [WARN] server.http_thread_pool_size 0 clamped to 1

This covers server.executor_threads, server.http_thread_pool_size,
server.keep_alive_timeout_sec, sse.max_clients and the subscription_executor.*
and data_provider.* knobs read in main.cpp.

The second read of http_thread_pool_size and sse.max_clients in main.cpp,
which only compares the pool against the SSE and cold-wait budget, keeps the
silent clamp on purpose. One typo should not produce two identical warnings.

clamp_thread_count and clamp_keep_alive_timeout stay silent because
gateway_core links no rclcpp. Their comments now say that reporting is the
caller's job.

An integration test launches one gateway below every floor and one above the
ceilings that are cheap to run at, and reads their own process output. The
floor gateway also has to serve /health, so a floor value that broke request
serving would fail the test instead of passing quietly.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
build: export a compile database from every package that lints

clang-tidy reads a file's include paths and flags from the compile database.
scripts/clang-tidy-diff.sh merges the per-package databases, and a file that is
not in the merged database is analysed with no flags at all. It then fails to
find its own headers, and the pre-push hook reports that parse error instead of
the checks it was meant to run. The warnings it prints in that state are not
real either: they come from a broken parse.

Eight of the 21 packages set CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS and the other 13 did
not, so most of the workspace was never analysed. Among them are opcua,
graph_watchdog and the integration test plugins.

The flag now lives in ROS2MedkitLinting.cmake, which 19 packages already
include. The two that do not, ros2_medkit_cmake and ros2_medkit_msgs, have no
C++ of their own. Including the module is now what makes a package lintable,
with nothing else to remember. The merged database grows from 9 databases and
416 entries to 17 and 583.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
build(gateway): register the new gtests with the domain-aware macro

main replaced medkit_set_test_domain with medkit_add_gtest. The new macro
registers the test and declares how many domains it needs in one call. The two
tests added on this branch still used the old macro, so after the rebase CMake
could not configure the package: the macro does not exist any more.

Both tests create ROS nodes and need one domain each, which is the default.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(gateway): word every cancel outcome for the verb the client used

One mapping is used by DELETE on an execution and by PUT with
{"capability":"stop"}. Several of its messages said "cancel" in every case.

A stop request against a dead action server was answered with "Cancel service
not available". Nothing in that message named what the client had asked for.
The timeout message said the server did not answer "the cancel request". The
branch for a goal that had already finished said "nothing left to cancel". The
branch for a return code that CancelGoal does not define passed the transport
message through as it was, and that message is worded as a cancel too.

Every branch now builds its message from the verb of the route. The lower case
form is derived from the same verb, so a call site cannot pass two words that
do not match.

A stop is carried out as an action cancel, so the ROS 2 name still has to
appear. It is now the reason after the verb, not the whole message: "Stop
failed: Cancel service not available". The transport message is kept because it
is the only part that says which service is missing, or which code the server
sent.

The new tests call the real handlers against the test cancel service. They also
check that each route passes its own verb.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(gateway): send the generic service request under the pending-request lock

The Humble compat client sent the request first, and inserted the promise into
the pending map after that. The caller runs on an HTTP thread. handle_response
runs on an executor thread. If the reply arrived in between, it found no entry
in the map, so it was dropped and the caller waited for the full timeout.

That window is short, but it is not always short. If the sending thread is
preempted right after the send, the window lasts as long as a scheduler slice.

The mutex is now taken before rcl_send_request and held until the promise is in
the map. The reply callback then has to wait for that entry. rclcpp uses the
same lock scope in Client::async_send_request_impl.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
test(integration): size the executor ceiling down under sanitizers

The TSan job SIGKILLed the sweep's ceiling gateway. The log shows why, and it
is not the OOM killer - launch_testing sent the signal itself after its own
escalation ran out: "failed to terminate '30' seconds after receiving 'SIGINT',
escalating to 'SIGTERM'", then "failed to terminate '45.0' seconds after
receiving 'SIGTERM', escalating to 'SIGKILL'". All six functional assertions
had already passed, including the /health request, so the gateway started,
applied its bound and served correctly; only joining 256 instrumented executor
threads outlived the grace period. Unsanitized the same teardown costs nothing
measurable - the whole test runs in about 1.3 s - so this is instrumentation
cost, not gateway behaviour, and the fix belongs in the harness rather than in
the documented range.

Resolve the upper endpoint per build: the documented 256 normally, 16 under a
sanitizer. Detection reads the sanitizer runtimes' own *SAN_OPTIONS so a future
sanitizer job cannot forget to opt in, with MEDKIT_TEST_SANITIZED as an
explicit override for reproducing locally; both jobs now set it as well.

The constant says plainly that a sanitized run does not pin the documented
ceiling and that every normal build still does, so nobody reads coverage into a
green sanitizer run that it does not have. The /health request stays, and the
pinned "Main executor bounded to %zu threads" wording is untouched.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message: style(integration): wrap the terminal-status poll predicate to the line limit

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
test: scale every wall-clock budget the sanitizer jobs run, not just one

MEDKIT_TEST_TIME_SCALE covered a single assertion while three more Python
budgets went unscaled and the C++ fixtures had no knob at all - and the
sanitizer jobs run the unit suite too. A knob that covers some budgets reads as
covering all of them, which is worse than not having one, because a flake in an
unscaled budget gets diagnosed as a product regression.

Cover the rest: the 256-thread gateway's /health deadline and per-request
timeout, the terminal-status polls, and the cancel fixture's service-discovery,
status-delivery and teardown budgets. Document the knob in CONTRIBUTING.md,
where someone reproducing a sanitizer failure will look for it - it had no
mention outside the workflow that sets it.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
docs(gateway): make the cancel contract answerable in the words it uses

The new 504 told clients to poll the execution status resource, but nothing
that resource documents can express a cancel outcome: it renders CANCELED and
ABORTED identically as "failed". The advice now names x-medkit.ros2_status,
which carries the ROS-level state verbatim, and rest.rst documents that field
and corrects the execution example, which named four keys the endpoint does not
emit and a status value that is not in its enum.

The terminal-status message quoted "succeeded"/"aborted" - raw ROS words the
resource it cites never produces. It now quotes that resource's own vocabulary,
and its test asserts the agreement rather than the string the handler happens
to print.

The 409 on re-executing a running execution carried invalid-request, which is
not in the SOVD standard code list, while the server already answers its other
409 with precondition-not-fulfilled ("prerequisites not met"). One status, one
code; the error table and the OpenAPI declaration follow, the latter having had
no 409 at all for a route that returns it.

If the goal is evicted between the mapper's read and the response body, the
202 no longer invents "running" for an execution whose own Location answers 404
- it says 404 too.

The parameter row claimed one budget for all four operation RPCs. Discovery
differs per RPC - bounded by the parameter for send goal, a fixed 2 s for get
result and cancel - so it now tabulates what each actually costs. The package
README documented cancel as 200 with a JSON body; it returns 204, and none of
the outcomes this branch added were there at all.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(gateway): subscribe to action status with the profile the protocol defines

The status stream is now the gateway's only source of truth for a goal's
terminal state, but it was subscribed KEEP_LAST(10) BEST_EFFORT VOLATILE while
rcl_action publishes it KEEP_LAST(1) RELIABLE TRANSIENT_LOCAL. The profiles
match, so the bug is not a mismatch - it is durability: the subscription is
created only after the goal has been sent, and a VOLATILE reader is delivered
nothing on match. An action that finishes inside that window published its
terminal frame to a reader that did not exist yet, and no other code path ever
re-reads a goal's status, so the execution reported "running" for the rest of
its life. Reproduced 2 runs in 3 with an immediate goal.

Use rcl_action's own profile, which is what it prescribes for the client side
too: the fresh subscription is delivered the writer's last sample on match,
which is exactly the frame it missed. KEEP_LAST(1) means the publisher
overwrites rather than blocking, so a slow gateway cannot stall an action
server; it can coalesce intermediate transitions, which is harmless because
only the current status is tracked.

The cancel fixture's stand-in publisher offered VOLATILE, which no action
server does and which a TRANSIENT_LOCAL reader cannot match - it now makes the
same offer as the server it stands in for.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(gateway): restore the status stream for a goal that races the unsubscribe

Vetoing the unsubscribe while a goal is tracked only covered the decision, not
the transport call that follows it with no lock held. A goal sent into that gap
re-flagged the path, got a no-op from the transport because the subscription
was still alive at that instant, and then had it destroyed by the unsubscribe
already in flight - leaving the goal tracked, the path flagged as subscribed,
and no status stream at all. Nothing repaired it, since the flag makes every
later subscribe a no-op, so the goal reported "running" until the stuck-goal
path evicted it with a warning blaming an action server that had done nothing
wrong, and every timed-out cancel for it answered 504 instead of reconciling.

Repair the pair after the transport call instead of holding the lock across
it: taking our mutex into rclcpp's subscription create/destroy path would add a
lock-order edge neither this method nor its subscribe sibling has today. The
header now states the postcondition that is actually true and testable - on
return, a path with a tracked goal has a live stream.

The fake transport gains the idempotence the real one has, so it can no longer
silently re-arm itself and hide the window, plus a one-shot re-entry hook that
reproduces the production interleaving with no threads.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(gateway): point the created-execution Location at the collection that was posted to

The 202 on POST executions built its Location from a hardcoded
apps-or-components pair, so on the areas and functions registrations of that
route - it is registered for all four entity types - a client was handed a
Location in the components collection, naming an entity that is not a
component. It also bypassed api_path(). The created execution is a
sub-resource of whatever collection the request targeted, so extend the
request path instead, matching the bulk-data and lock handlers.

Exercising this needs a genuine non-component entity that owns the action,
because create_execution rejects a collection/entity-type mismatch before it
gets that far, so the handler fixture now also seeds the area its component
sits in.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
refactor(gateway): bind the stop Location to the request path without copying

req.path() already returns a const reference; the reconciled 202 branch was
copy-constructing a std::string from it on every accepted stop.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(log_bridge): take the cooldown timestamp by const reference

rclcpp::Time was copied on every ERROR/FATAL log line only to be read, which
clang-tidy flags as performance-unnecessary-value-param.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(gateway): state the cancel precondition instead of guarding against it

Two of the three guards in cancel_action_goal cannot be tripped by a caller
that honours the method's contract: both HTTP entry points resolve the
execution through get_tracked_goal and answer 404 themselves, every tracked
goal_id is produced by uuid_bytes_to_hex, and the action transport is a
constructor dependency the gateway always supplies. Giving the malformed-id
guard its own wire status was therefore covering an input no caller can
build, so drop it and write the precondition down on the declaration
instead. The tracked-goal re-check keeps its classification: that one a
caller genuinely can trip, by racing the cleanup timer.

Pin the surviving consequence end to end as well - after a cancel, the
execution must reach a terminal ROS 2 status rather than sitting in
"canceling" forever, which is the only place the stream-versus-RPC ordering
is visible over HTTP.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
test(integration): scale in-test budgets under sanitizers, pin the clamped executor

The sanitizer jobs multiply every declared CTest timeout, but a budget a test
asserts on itself is invisible to that rewrite: an instrumented gateway can
blow "must answer within 8s" long before ctest's clock runs out, and the
failure reads as a starved response rather than as ASan/TSan overhead. Read
the multiplier from MEDKIT_TEST_TIME_SCALE, which those two jobs now set to
the same factor they apply to ctest. The unscaled value stays 8s so the
falsifier keeps its edge where it was proven red - no scaling turns burning
the full 10s service budget and answering 500 into a pass.

The executor_threads clamp sweep asserted only startup log lines, so a
regression that logged the clamped count and then failed to bring the
executor up would have stayed green. Add one real request against the
256-thread gateway.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(gateway): bound service_call_timeout_sec and document the cancel budget

With the 15s cancel floor gone this parameter is the whole cancel budget,
yet it was declared with no range at all and appeared in no document. Zero
and negatives were accepted silently and make the response wait expire
immediately, so every cancel answers 504 unless the status stream wins the
race; an unbounded value pins an HTTP worker for as long as it says. Clamp
to [1, 3600] with a warning, like the sibling timeouts, and pin the whole
config space - both degenerate directions, both endpoints and the default -
against the budget the gateway actually applies rather than the value that
was configured.

Document the parameter next to its siblings in the server config table and
define "cancel budget" where the DELETE/PUT route text uses it: the
configured timeout plus up to 2s of cancel-service discovery, which a
shorter budget does not shorten. Also correct the Common Error Codes table,
where invalid-request was listed as 400-only thirty lines under the PUT
block that documents it on 409.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(gateway): answer every cancel outcome with what the gateway knows

The action status stream is the authority for a goal's state, but the RPC
completions were still writing over it. An accepted CancelGoal wrote
CANCELING unconditionally, so a stream frame carrying the terminal CANCELED
that arrived first was moved backwards permanently: no further frame is ever
published, GET kept reporting the goal as running, and it only left the
tracking map through the stuck-goal path with a false "action server crashed"
warning. update_goal_status now refuses to leave a terminal state - the guard
belongs there rather than at the cancel call site because goal-accept and
get_result can land late in exactly the same way, while the stream keeps
writing directly under the lock.

For the same reason a tracked goal must never lose its status stream:
cleanup reads the goal count for a path and unsubscribes afterwards, so a
goal sent in between kept a subscription that was about to be destroyed, and
since the cancel-timeout path reconciles against that stream such a goal
could only ever answer 504. unsubscribe_from_action_status now re-checks
under the lock that guards the erase and lets a live goal veto it.

The manager's three cancel guards never classified themselves and rode the
kTransportError default into 500 "action server unavailable" - including for
an execution the cleanup timer evicted between the handler's lookup and the
manager's re-check, where the truthful answer is the 404 the same request
gets a millisecond later. They now carry kNotTracked (404) and
kInvalidRequest (400); only the missing-transport guard keeps 500. The
mapper is declared in the header so those wire mappings are pinned directly:
over HTTP they are reachable only through a race.

Also on the response shapes: the reconciled 202 body rendered a hardcoded
"running" although the reconcile set includes CANCELED, which an immediate
GET of the same execution reports as "failed"; it now renders the tracked
status. Its Location header was built from a hardcoded apps/components pair
and sent areas and functions clients into the components collection; it now
echoes the request path. A timed-out cancel on a goal the gateway already
knows to be terminal no longer promises progress that cannot happen, and
error parameters carry return_code only when a server actually returned one.
The per-return_code wording for codes 1-3 now exists once, in the mapper -
the transport's second copy meant deleting a mapper case silently changed
the wire message with every test still green.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(log_bridge): read integer parameters as int64 before narrowing

declare_parameter<int>() takes the int64 a ROS parameter actually holds and
narrows it on the way in, which -Wconversion flags and which lets an
out-of-range severity_floor or max_tracked_nodes wrap before its own range
check ever runs. Read both as int64, clamp in that domain, and narrow after.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
perf(gateway): take the freeze-frame fault event by const reference

clang-tidy (performance-unnecessary-value-param) flags the FaultEvent
shared_ptr being copied on every subscription callback invocation while
only read as const. Pass it by const reference.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(gateway): report a timed-out action cancel as unknown outcome, not rejection

A CancelGoal round-trip that produced no response was collapsed into the
same 400 x-medkit-ros2-action-rejected error as a definitive server
rejection, and the tracked execution status was never reconciled with the
/_action/status stream - the client was told the cancel was refused while
the goal was in fact cancelling (issue #576).

ActionCancelResult now carries an explicit CancelOutcome set by the
transport at every exit, and both cancel entry points (DELETE execution
and PUT-stop) share one mapping helper:

- timeout: consult the tracked goal fed by the /_action/status stream -
  if it already shows CANCELING/CANCELED the cancellation is in progress
  (204, or 202 for PUT-stop); otherwise 504 with the standard SOVD
  not-responding code and a message pointing at the execution status
  resource. Tracked status is never hand-written on this path - the
  status stream stays the authority.
- cancel service unavailable: 503 x-medkit-ros2-action-unavailable
- transport failure: 500 x-medkit-ros2-action-unavailable
- server rejection (return_code 1/2/3): 400
  x-medkit-ros2-action-rejected, unchanged

The 15s cancel budget floor is removed: cancel uses
service_call_timeout_sec like every other action RPC - with timeouts
reported honestly and reconciled against the status stream, the floor no
longer papers over anything. The execution cancel/stop routes declare
their real status codes in OpenAPI and the REST docs, and the stale
Common Error Codes table now matches the implemented constants
(phantom ERR_TIMEOUT/ERR_INVALID_INPUT/ERR_OPERATION_FAILED/
ERR_INVALID_ENTITY_ID rows replaced, not-responding -> 504 added).

Covered by unit-fixture falsifiers driving a raw CancelGoal service that
swallows or rejects requests (timeout -> 504 with tracked status
untouched, stream-reconciled timeout -> 204/202, rejection -> 400 for
both entry points) and an integration test that kills the action server
mid-goal and expects 503. The handler-level stop test now asserts the
mapped 504 instead of the never-produced ERR_VENDOR_ERROR.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(gateway): dispatch blocking-RPC responses on a shared reentrant callback group

server.executor_threads was decorative for RPC-response parallelism: the
generic service clients, the per-action client trio, and the per-action
status subscriptions all landed in the node default MutuallyExclusive
callback group, so one long discovery refresh pass (e.g. a peer
aggregation health check) stalled every in-flight service/action response
regardless of the configured thread count - the response then surfaced as
a bogus service timeout after the full budget (issue #575).

Move the blocking-RPC clients (generic service clients + the per-action
send_goal/get_result/cancel_goal trio) to one shared Reentrant group and
the per-action /_action/status subscriptions to a dedicated
MutuallyExclusive group - in-order delivery preserved, decoupled from the
default group. Groups are created once at startup by a ros2_common
factory (the issue #375 gate bans create_callback_group outside
ros2_common/) and injected into the transports as constructor
dependencies; the compat shim registers Humble clients into the passed
group. Timers and the SSE-fault/trigger-fault/rosout subscriptions stay
in the default group by design: refresh passes must remain serialized and
those subscriptions rely on in-order delivery.

Covered by an executor-starvation falsifier (black-hole aggregation peer
keeps a refresh pass permanently in flight; a service-backed operation
must still complete fast), a single-thread no-deadlock guard, an
executor_threads clamp sweep over the documented [1, 256] range, and a
unit pin of the group wiring itself.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(fault_manager): stop losing a cleared fault's cleanup and an over-cap fault's data

A fault cleared while its own recording was still being opened kept a row.
on_fault_cleared() removes the code from the recording state only if the guard
was already set when the clear arrived, and auto-cleanup finds no row yet, so
the finalise inserts one afterwards and nothing is left to remove it - the bag
stays referenced for good. The finalise asks the store whether each fault is
still uncleared instead of trusting a flag captured earlier. A fault the store
does not know keeps its row: unknown is not cleared.

Past the 32 fault attachment cap, an over-cap fault in entity mode got neither a
row nor its own data. The cap is meant to withhold the lookup key only - that is
what its comment and the configuration page both say - but the code returned
before the scope was widened, so the recording never learned that fault's topics
and dropped every message it published.

The entity scope is resolved after the cheap check for "this fault already owns
the running recording", not before it. Moving the resolution off the recording
lock had put a fault-store read and a graph enumeration in front of that
early-out, which a level-triggered reporter pays on every repeat.

Three coverage gaps close with them: a backend throwing something that is not a
std::exception, which the storage interface permits; repeated confirmations
costing no scope resolution; and the clock arithmetic at values far enough apart
to overflow a signed subtraction.

One test was written and removed again. It made the bag's parent directory
read-only so the discard's removal would fail, which works for a normal user and
not for root, and CI runs the suite as root. Nothing portable makes remove_all
fail there, so that path has no test and the pull request says so.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
build: stop the pre-push clang-tidy from analysing the base branch's files

On the pre-push stage pre-commit hands the hook everything that differs between
the local branch and the REMOTE branch. After a rebase the remote tip is the
pre-rebase one, so every file the base branch moved in the meantime arrives
looking changed. A branch rebased over twenty-seven commits handed it thirteen
files in three packages nobody had touched, and the push was rejected for two of
them - not over their contents, but because their packages were not built in
that worktree and clang-tidy without a compile database reports the whole file
as errors.

The list is narrowed to what the branch actually changes, against its merge base
with origin/main, which is what "changed files only" was meant to be. When that
base cannot be resolved - a fresh clone, a detached checkout, a fork whose remote
is not called origin - the filter is skipped rather than quietly passing
everything. Files named directly on the command line still go through unchanged.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(fault_manager): close the ordering and atomicity holes around the handover

Dropping the entity filter before taking the writer opens a window of its own.
A subscription callback reads the recording guard, then consults the filter,
then takes the writer lock. One that already passed the guard can find the
filter emptied underneath it, read the empty set as "write everything", and
append a topic belonging to no covered fault to the bag being closed. Taking
the writer first closes that: past it active_writer_ is null, so a late callback
writes nowhere.

The immediate path had the same mistake in the other direction. It reset the
writer and then measured, but dropping the last reference runs ~Writer - the bag
flush and the metadata.yaml write - and reset() returns only once that is done.
It takes the writer out under the lock, measures, and closes afterwards.

store_rows_or_discard_bag() promised never to throw while catching
std::exception only. The storage interface says nothing about what a backend
throws, and this path reaches a noexcept destructor. It catches everything now.
A discard that cannot remove the directory says what is left behind instead of
reporting a discard that did not happen.

The in-memory backend's batch store is all-or-nothing. The base implementation
is a plain loop, so a backend using it can store half a burst and then throw,
and the discard would delete the bag those stored rows name. The batch is built
beside the live map and swapped in, and the base class documents that
all-or-nothing is required. Replaced bags are unlinked on the finished batch:
judged row by row beforehand, two faults sharing the bag being replaced each see
the other still pointing at it and neither unlinks it.

Resolving a fault's entity scope no longer happens under the recording lock. It
reads the fault store, whose busy timeout is five seconds, then queries the graph
twice per topic, and the finalise of the window being attached to needs the same
lock - so an attaching fault could hold that window open for as long as either
stalled.

bounded_history_ns() saturates its clock differences. It is public and takes two
clocks nothing here controls, so a pair far enough apart was signed overflow
before the bound could apply.

Where the empty-buffer boundary actually happens is now documented. The broad
topic modes subscribe to /fault_manager/events, so reporting a fault refills the
ring buffer and the next fault of a burst usually finds history. The case
belongs mostly to a narrowed capture. The launch test excludes that topic, which
is the only way to reach the boundary in a broad mode.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(fault_manager): keep bags, rows and durations honest when something fails

Several failure paths said one thing and did another.

A throw from the quota sweep deleted the bag that had just been stored.
store_rosbag_files() commits before it returns, so the rows were already
durable, and the directory they named was removed under them. Retrieval then
failed for good and the bytes kept counting against max_total_storage_mb, which
sums rows, so the quota that triggered the sweep never recovered. Both
finalisation paths now use one store-or-discard step: a failing store discards
the recording, because nothing could reach it, and a failing sweep keeps the bag
and its rows. The sweep runs under its own handler that only logs, because this
code is reached from stop() and so from a noexcept destructor.

The duration_after_sec == 0 path had no handler at all, so a throwing store left
a directory with no row: unreachable, uncounted, and impossible to evict.

delete_rosbag_file() unlinked the directory before running its DELETE. That
statement throws on a busy or full database, and the surviving row then named a
bag that was gone. It now deletes the row first, which its batch sibling already
did.

The entity filter is dropped with the recording it belongs to. Cleared after the
handover lock, it landed on the next recording instead, and an empty filter
means "write everything", so a boundary recording quietly became a capture of
the whole graph - in "entity", which is the default mode.

duration_sec stops being measured when the writer leaves the write path.
Closing the bag and walking its directory for a size are the fault manager's own
time, and charging them to the recording made a stored duration grow with how
slow the disk was.

The buffered history a flush may claim is capped at how long the capture has
been running. Message ages are wall-clock differences applied to a monotonic
origin, so a clock step between buffering and flushing went into the figure in
full, and one larger than the machine's uptime drove the origin below zero,
which is read as "never started" and reported as a duration of zero.

arm_post_fault_timer() no longer takes a period it cannot honour. On the re-arm
branch reset() restarts the period the timer was built with, and
duration_after_sec is read once at construction and never changes.

The tests for all of this were each run against the code without its fix. Two
needed the instrument fixed first: the metadata double failed only the batch
entry point while the immediate path called the single-row one, and the race
test could not see the filter at all because it ran in "topics: all".

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(fault_manager): give the fault at a recording-window boundary its own bag

During a post-fault window the capture writes messages straight to the bag and
stops filling the ring buffer. The flush that started the window already
emptied that buffer. So a fault confirmed a few milliseconds after the window
closes finds an empty buffer. flush_to_bag() returned an empty path, the caller
only logged a warning, no row was written, and nothing tried again. GetRosbag
then failed for that fault forever.

That is the case the feature exists for. Faults arrive in bursts from one root
cause, and the second fault of a burst is the one that lands in this gap.

When the buffer is empty and duration_after_sec > 0, the capture now opens a
writer anyway and records the post-fault window alone. An empty buffer and a
failed open are two different results, so no post-roll is started on top of an
I/O failure.

The recording state changes hands in one critical section. Releasing the guard
and reaching for the writer afterwards left a gap where an incoming
confirmation installed its writer and the outgoing finalise then destroyed it:
every message dropped, and a row stored for the empty bag.

The post-fault timer is re-armed instead of being created again per recording,
so no timer is destroyed on the executor thread while another is created on the
capture pool.

The SQLite statement wrappers declare their move operations, which they already
relied on not having.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
test: allocate a DDS domain for each test when it starts

A test takes its ROS_DOMAIN_ID when it starts and holds it, through an open
TCP socket on 32768 + domain, for exactly as long as it runs. The lock is
domain_coordinator.domain_id from ament_cmake_ros, which ships on every distro
this project builds for. Release is the kernel closing the socket, so a crash
and a SIGKILL free the domain the same way an ordinary exit does.

This replaces a hand-written table of per-package domain pools. The pools had
to stay pairwise disjoint because colcon runs a separate ctest per package and
a CTest RESOURCE_LOCK only binds inside one ctest run. An OS-level lock has no
such boundary, so both the table and the disjointness requirement go with it.
Adding a test no longer requires touching domain allocation anywhere.

The guard is armed in every package without the package asking. An earlier
shape had each package register it; four never did, and their tests ran on
domain 0 with nothing to say so.

Details that are not obvious:

- A test needing several domains takes them all at once or none. Taking them
  one at a time and holding each while waiting for the next lets two such
  tests each hold part of what the other needs. That trades a deadlock for a
  bounded livelock, paid for by a fresh randomly started selector per attempt
  and a jittered backoff.
- The band is refused, not narrowed, when it does not hold against
  net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range on the machine running the tests. A run quietly
  reduced to ten domains reads as flaky timeouts rather than as a host that
  needs configuring. MEDKIT_TEST_DOMAIN_BAND takes the safe subset on purpose.
- The wait for a free domain is derived from each test's own TIMEOUT, and a
  registration whose wait does not fit inside its timeout is rejected. With a
  fixed 180 s wait against ament's 60 s default, CTest killed the test before
  the allocator could ever report why it failed.
- The wrapper reserves a failing result file naming itself before it does
  anything that can fail, and imports only the standard library at module
  scope, so a missing dependency leaves a visible failure instead of no file.
- Shared lint configs are files of ros2_medkit_cmake, installed next to its
  CMake modules, with the repository root paths as symlinks into it. Reaching
  the repository root cannot work in a binary package build, which unpacks one
  package. Resolution fails loudly rather than skipping the check.
- ros2_medkit_cmake is declared NONE, and with no language enabled CMake
  leaves CMAKE_LIBRARY_ARCHITECTURE empty, so find_library never searches the
  multiarch directory. On Humble that makes launch_testing_ament_cmake fail at
  FindPythonLibs, so the launch test lives in a package that compiles.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
test: drop stale result files before a run

`colcon test-result` reads whatever it finds under the build base, so a run
that tests one package still reported totals in the thousands from earlier
runs. The CTest directories alone produce a total with no file on disk behind
it, which reads as a passing suite that never ran.

It matches no naming convention either. Its xunit extension walks the whole
tree, parses every .xml file and counts the testsuite and testsuites roots, so
a sweep written against one suffix drifts from it: deleting *.xunit.xml only
removed 6 files out of 177 on a real build tree, because ament_add_gtest
writes <target>.gtest.xml.

The sweep therefore asks colcon itself. It removes exactly what colcon would
have counted and leaves the build inputs alone; about 230 .xml files here are
node set definitions that a wider find would have deleted. Testing/ goes
separately, because the ctest side only offers its TAG file for deletion.

It lives in its own script so it can be run and tested on its own.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(graph_watchdog): keep ROS entities off the gateway executor

graph_watchdog creates its lifecycle-event subscriptions and its ReportFault
client on the shared gateway node, in the node's default callback group. The
gateway executor collects entities in that group, and rclcpp::AnyExecutable
holds a strong reference to whatever it dispatches while that reference lives
as a local on the executor thread. That makes the executor thread a routine
holder of the last reference to a subscription or a client, so its destructor
can run there, and ~Subscription / ~Client mutate the node's rcl entity
registry. Nothing in the watcher's own locking reaches an executor thread, so
that mutation can run concurrently with another component creating an entity
on the same node, corrupting the registry both sides share.

The fix is the same in both places: put the entity in a callback group of the
watchdog's own, created with automatically_add_to_executor_with_node disabled,
and add that group only to a private SingleThreadedExecutor owned by the
plugin. No gateway executor ever sees these entities, so creation, callback
execution and destruction all happen on the plugin's own tick thread, which
drains the private executor in short slices between ticks and destroys it
before the entity it owns in shutdown() so the last reference is released
there, under the node mutex, deterministically. For the fault client this also
fixes a real leak: raise_fault discards every future, but rclcpp keeps
per-request state until an executor processes the response, so a client left
unpumped on the gateway executor accumulated one pending entry per raised
fault for the life of the process.

The same class of bug showed up in a test fixture: test_param_drift_integration
created and dropped a throwaway parameter-service client on every call while a
MultiThreadedExecutor was spinning on another thread, so the last reference to
a dropped client was often released on that executor thread instead of the
caller's, running its destructor concurrently with the next client creation on
the same node. The fixture now caches one client per service name and only
releases them in TearDown, after the executor has stopped spinning and the
nodes have been removed from it.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
test(opcua): run the secured A&C fault manager on memory storage

Point the secured OPC UA integration test's fault_manager_node at
storage_type:=memory instead of the default sqlite file. The test starts and
tears down a fresh fault manager per run, and a leftover database file from a
previous run (or a previous test on a reused domain) could carry faults or
confirmation state into a run that expects to start clean.

test_opcua_secured was also drawing its ROS_DOMAIN_ID from a scratch range
outside the shared pool table instead of a real pool domain, and the domain
scan in check_test_domains.py iterated packages in whatever order os.listdir
returned, which is not deterministic and made cross-package overlap
detection depend on filesystem order. Both are fixed here: the test now
reserves a domain from the ros2_medkit_opcua pool through
medkit_reserve_test_domain, and the scan sorts the package list before
comparing pools.

Two more leaks came out of running the test repeatedly on the same domain.
A ros2cli daemon started by a `ros2 topic` call inside the test outlives the
test process unless it is explicitly killed, and it keeps the domain's DDS
resources alive for the next test that reuses it; the test now tears the
daemon down itself instead of relying on process exit. Guard a PID-reuse
edge case too: checking a captured server PID with `kill -0` is not enough
once enough time has passed for the PID to be recycled by an unrelated
process, so the check now also confirms the process command line still
matches the alarm server before treating it as still running.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(opcua): build the package without compiler warnings

The package compiled with 37 warnings under -Wall -Wextra -Wconversion.
No gate fails on them, so they accumulated.

slugify() and short_hash_hex() iterated a std::string as
'for (unsigned char c : s)'. The element type is char, so every iteration
performed an implicit char -> unsigned char conversion and -Wsign-conversion
fired. The unsigned char is required: std::isalnum and std::toupper are
undefined for a negative char. The conversion is now explicit, matching
address_space_browser.cpp in this package.

readAccessLevel() and readUserAccessLevel() already return the underlying
uint8_t of the bitmask, so the static_cast<uint8_t> around them was a
no-op that tripped -Wuseless-cast. Dropping it also means a future widening
of that underlying type surfaces as -Wconversion instead of being cast away
silently.

The two test doubles aggregate-initialised LockAccessResult and LockError
with fewer initialisers than members, leaving denied_code and
existing_lock_id to -Wmissing-field-initializers. Both now list every
member, as the graph_provider, topic_beacon and param_beacon doubles do.
status_code is written as 409, the value it defaulted to.

The concurrency test dropped the nodiscard result of clear_fault(). That is
intentional - it races the shared pending-report buffer and asserts on no
single clear - so the discard is now explicit and says why.

slugify() and short_hash_hex() are on the fault_code path. Both were checked
against their previous versions over every single byte and every ordered
byte pair, 65792 inputs, with no difference in output.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
fix(test): keep test DDS domains out of the kernel ephemeral port range

RTPS gives a DDS domain the UDP slice [7400 + 250*d, 7400 + 250*d + 249], and
both CycloneDDS and Fast-DDS bind inside it without SO_REUSEPORT. The kernel
hands out ephemeral ports from net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, 32768-60999 by
default, and most of the domains we handed to tests sat inside it. When
another process on the machine got one of those ports first, every node on
the domain failed to start with "failed to bind to ANY:<port>: address in
use", and the test reported "Launch stopped before the active tests
finished", which says nothing about the cause.

Only domains 1-100 and 215-231 have a slice that sits entirely outside the
default ephemeral range. Domain 101 is excluded too: its slice, 32650-32899,
already overlaps the range starting at 32768. Domain 232 is excluded because
its slice runs past 65535. Domain 0 is left alone for the developer shell.

That is fewer domains than we have test slots for, so a package pool now
wraps around and two of its tests can share a domain. medkit_set_test_domain
also puts a medkit_dds_domain_<id> RESOURCE_LOCK on the test, so CTest never
runs two of them at the same time; that lock is what makes the reuse safe,
since scripts/test.sh runs ctest -j $(nproc) and tests inside one package
really do run concurrently otherwise.

Move the pools into one table in ROS2MedkitTestDomain.cmake so a package
names itself instead of repeating a range, and the allocation can no longer
drift between the module and a CMakeLists.txt. Two checks guard the scheme
from there on: at configure time the module validates the whole table, not
just the pool being asked for, checking every slice against the live
/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range, pools pairwise disjoint, and domain 0
rejected; at test time, test_dds_domain_allocation reads the generated CTest
properties back and checks them against the same live range, which also
catches a hand-written ROS_DOMAIN_ID and a resource lock dropped by a
property overwrite. Both properties are appended rather than set outright,
so a handful of call sites that used to set RESOURCE_LOCK after the domain
assignment were changed to set_property(... APPEND ...).

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
build(graph_watchdog): enable flake8 for the package's Python files

Removes ament_cmake_flake8 from AMENT_LINT_AUTO_EXCLUDE so graph_watchdog's
e2e test scripts run through the same check as the rest of the tree; only
pep257 stays excluded, deferred with the docstring backlog documented in
ros2_medkit_integration_tests. Also skips ament_cmake_flake8 in the
Dockerfile's rosdep key list, since the image build runs with
BUILD_TESTING=OFF and never installs or uses the linter.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
docs: correct stale and overstated claims about Python lint coverage

The ros2_medkit_integration_tests CMakeLists comment counted 563
docstrings that put their summary on the opening line and claimed
every other package in the tree runs ament_pep257. The real count is
559, and ros2_medkit_graph_watchdog is the one package that still
excludes both flake8 and pep257 for its Python files.

The same comment also claimed the pre-commit hook installing the
plugins ament_flake8 depends on means nothing the gate rejects can
pass the hook. CI installs those plugins from apt while the hook's
additional_dependencies are unpinned and resolve from PyPI, so the
comment now states plugin coverage rather than an outcome guarantee.
The pre-commit config comment had a matching grammar slip and did not
say that the hook only checks the files a commit touches, unlike
quality.yml, which lints the whole package.

The ros2_medkit_graph_watchdog CMakeLists comment said no package in
the workspace lints Python. ros2_medkit_integration_tests now does, so
the comment is rewritten to say this package is the last one still
excluding those checks.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
style(graph_watchdog): fix docstring, import-order and line-length findings in e2e tests

These four e2e test files carried findings that predate this branch. Running
flake8 with only D, I and E selected against the files as they stood at
930ca5db reproduces the same 15 findings fixed here: 4 D205, 1 D209, 4 D400,
2 E501 and 4 I100. Selecting Q, A and C4 against the same content finds
nothing, so none of this is fallout from adding flake8-builtins,
flake8-comprehensions or flake8-quotes to the pre-commit hook in the previous
commit. D comes from flake8-docstrings and I from flake8-import-order, both
already installed in the hook before that change.

pre-commit only runs flake8 against files that are part of a commit, so
nothing had exercised these four files since those two plugins were added.
`pre-commit run flake8 --all-files` is what finally scanned them and turned up
the findings fixed here: module and class docstring summaries reshaped into a
single, period-terminated sentence on the opening line with a blank line
before the description; the harness import in each file annotated with
`# noqa: E402, I100` and the same explanation already used in
test_param_drift_e2e.test.py, since the sys.path.insert one line above makes
the import order this checker wants impossible; and two lines wrapped under
the 99 column limit.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
build: run the CI flake8 plugins in the pre-commit hook too

The hook installed blind-except, class-newline, docstrings and import-order.
ament_flake8 depends on builtins, comprehensions, docstrings, import-order and
quotes. So Q, A and C4 ran in quality.yml and nowhere locally, and a file could
pass every hook and then turn CI red.

The hook now installs all five ament_flake8 has, keeping the two it already had
on top. That makes it a superset rather than a match: blind-except and
class-newline stay local-only because ament_flake8 comments both out of its
package.xml. The comment in the integration tests CMakeLists said the rule sets
matched; it now says what is actually true.

data.author: Bartosz Burda
data.message:
style(repo): quote style and dict literals in the root Python

scripts/ and docs/ sit outside every ROS package, so no ament_flake8 run has
ever checked them, and the pre-commit hook lacks the quote, builtins and
comprehensions plugins that would have. Both files had drifted from the style
the rest of the tree is held to: 198 double-quoted literals and 4 dict() calls
in place of literals.

Quotes were converted with a tokenizer pass that skips any literal containing
a quote or a backslash, so no escaping decision is ever made automatically.
That left 36 literals to convert by hand: 10 f-strings, which the tokenizer
does not expose as plain STRING tokens, and 26 non-f-string literals the
